Lead and Coal Studies
 
INTRODUCTION 
This report documents the Existing Traffic Analysis, Speed Limit Reduction Alternative Analysis, Single-Lane 
Alternative Analysis, and Conversion to Two-Way Streets Alternative Analysis for the Lead and Coal 
Avenues Study in Albuquerque, NM. Per the guidelines provided in the Highway Capacity Manual (HCM), 
delay and level of service results were obtained to assess Lead and Coal Avenues from Broadway Boulevard 
to Washington Street as is. The Synchro 12 analysis software was used to conduct this analysis.  
STUDY ORIGINS 
Residents near Lead and Coal Avenues are profoundly concerned about road safety, mainly due to frequent 
crashes that damage property near the roadway. These crashes often involve vehicles colliding with walls, 
homes, and other structures adjacent to the road, making residents perceive an unsafe environment for 
pedestrian or bicyclist travel. In response to these safety issues, a study was conducted in 2007 to explore 
how road design could improve livability in the area, which led to a corridor redesign in 2012. 
Despite these changes, safety concerns persisted among residents in the years following the redesign. This 
prompted the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) to conduct a road safety audit (RSA) in June 2022 
with the assistance of the Mid-Region Council of Governments (MRCOG). The RSA identified 19 
recommendations to enhance safety; four initiatives were advanced for further study. 
In November 2022, the Lead and Coal Working Group was established to facilitate dialogue between 
residents, the Mayor’s administration, the City of Albuquerque’s Department of Municipal Development, 
the District 6 City Councilor, and the Albuquerque Police Department. This forum allowed residents to voice 
their concerns and discuss the future of the corridors with city officials, ultimately leading to the initiation 
of this study. 
This study builds on the RSA by providing a detailed analysis of the four initiatives: Reducing the Posted 
Speed Limit to 25 MPH, Single-Lane operation, Two-way Operation, and a Noise Assessment. The Lead and 
Coal Taskforce was created to offer input and compare the study's quantitative findings with residents’ 
qualitative experiences to enhance community involvement. The task force met with the project team 
biweekly to stay informed and provide feedback. 
This report documents the study's findings to guide the Lead and Coal Working Group in making informed 
decisions about the future of these corridors.

STUDY AREA 
The study area extends from Broadway Boulevard east to Washington Street along Lead Avenue and Coal 
Avenue in Albuquerque, New Mexico. During the scoping meeting, Lead Avenue and Coal Avenue 
intersections from Broadway Boulevard through Washington Street were identified for analysis.

DEMOGRAPHICS AND SOCIOECONOMIC PROFILE 
Census tracts within one-half mile of the study corridor comprise the study area statistics. The Census 
Tracts comprise 5.03, 5.04, 11.01, 11.02, 12.01, 12.02, 14, 15, 17.01, 17.02, 18, 20, 21, and 49. The study 
area is in the southeast quadrant of Albuquerque, NM, with a population of 37,871. The median household 
income in the study area is $46,157, below the median income in city, county, and statewide. The 
percentage of the population with a disability is 17.3% within the study area, exceeding the city, county, 
and state. At 11.1%, the rate of households without a vehicle within the study area is greater than the city, 
county, and state rates, though the employment rate of 60.7% is above average.

PREVIOUS AND CONCURRENT STUDIES AND PLANS 
Solutions for Albuquerque’s Traffic Problems: A Comprehensive Program (1950) 
A comprehensive study of Albuquerque’s traffic issues was conducted in 1950 to provide recommendations 
ranging from signal timings to arterial street plans. The study offers recommendations for traffic 
ordinances, traffic engineering, arterial systems, parking, truck operations, public transit, traffic safety, 
zoning, and enforcement on a city-wide level.  
New Vision for Lead & Coal Avenues (2007) 
In 2005-06, following continued concerns regarding the impact of Lead & Coal Avenues on their 
neighborhoods, Wilson & Company assessed the corridor, a public involvement meeting was held, and a 
Stakeholder’s Task Force was formed.  Two recommendations were presented to city administration by the 
Task Force, both involving reducing the number of lanes on each roadway from three to two throughout 
the corridor.  The options were to make Lead & Coal Avenues two-way roadways with one driving lane in 
each direction or one-way roadways, each with two driving lanes, and the addition of a bicycle lane.   
Both recommendations were intended to reduce speeds, make the corridor more accessible to bicyclists 
and pedestrians, reduce accidents and traffic volumes, widen sidewalks, and meet ADA requirements.  
Other recommendations were also presented, including lighting, pedestrian pushbuttons, lane width 
restrictions, radar speed signs, red light cameras at signalized intersections, and quiet asphalt.   
Road Safety Audit of Lead and Coal Avenues (Broadway Blvd. to Washington St.) (2019) 
In 2019, the City of Albuquerque and a multidisciplinary team conducted a Road Safety Audit (RSA) of the 
Lead and Coal Avenue corridors between Broadway Boulevard and Washington Street. A total of 19 findings 
were graded on a scale of A through F, where the letter grades represent a priority level based on Crash 
Frequency and Crash Severity. The team concluded that the corridors present a variety of issues related to 
motorist behavior, corridor design, and infrastructure age and condition.  
Lead Avenue and Coal Avenue Rest-in-Red Feasibility Study (2021) 
The Lead Avenue and Coal Avenue Rest-in-Red Feasibility Study was conducted in 2021 to assess the impact 
and operations of a Rest-in-red scheme on Lead Avenue and Coal Avenue. Implementing Enhanced Rest-in-
Red for these corridors was intended to aid with speed compliance and reduce crashes and crash severity, 
ultimately improving the quality of life of the residential areas on these corridors. The study recommended 
that Rest-in-red operations be implemented during the off-peak hours to start and adjust as needed. 
City of Albuquerque 2024 Bikeway and Trail Facilities Plan (2024) 
The City of Albuquerque produced a Bikeway and Trail Facilities Plan in 2024 to better manage the growth 
of the bikeway trail systems and ensure a safe and enjoyable experience for non-motorized users. 
Recommendations from this plan include bikeway facilities and crossing treatments to encourage people to 
choose bicycling as a mode of transportation. 
Connections 2040 Metropolitan Transportation Plan (2020) 
The Connections 2040 Metropolitan Transportation Plan was adopted in 2020. Its goal was to improve the 
efficiency of the movement of people and goods. The Mid-Region Council of Governments (MRCOG) 
provided a long-range plan for zoning, roadway networks, and other crucial infrastructure. It identifies gaps 
in the existing systems to give purpose and needs for work done in 2040.

Lead and Coal Studies
 
EXISTING CONDITIONS 
ROADWAY CHARACTERISTICS 
Lead and Coal Avenues form a one-way couplet, with Coal running east and Lead running west. They are 
two-lane, one-way streets maintained by the City of Albuquerque. Between Broadway Boulevard and 
Washington Street, they comprise two 11-foot travel lanes; travel lanes narrow in some areas near 
intersections with auxiliary turn lanes. Pedestrian and bicycle facilities are present throughout the Lead and 
Coal corridors in the form of ADA-compliant sidewalks and bicycle lanes.  
SIGNALIZED INTERSECTIONS 
The following details are the traffic control and characteristics of the existing intersections in the study 
area: 
Lead Avenue & Broadway Boulevard is a four-legged, three-way, signalized intersection. The east approach 
consists of a left-turn lane, two through lanes, and a right-turn lane. The north approach consists of two 
through lanes and a right-turn lane, while the south approach consists of a left-turn lane and two through 
lanes. Marked crossings, pedestrian signals, non-directional curb ramps, and detectable warning surfaces 
(DWS) are present at each leg of the intersection. DWS provides tactile feedback to alert pedestrians with 
visual impairments to curb ramps, pedestrian crossings, and transit stops. The marked crossing on the north 
leg of the intersection is disrupted by a median that does not appear to be used as a pedestrian refuge 
island.  
Lead Avenue and Walter Street is a four-legged, three-way, signalized intersection. The east approach 
consists of two through lanes, while the north and south approaches each consist of a through lane. 
Marked crossings, pedestrian signals, and DWS are present at each leg of the intersection. Directional curb 
ramps are present on the south corners, while non-directional curb ramps are present on the north 
corners.  
Lead Avenue Cedar Street, Buena Vista Drive, Columbia Drive, and Wellesley Drive are four-legged, three-
way, signalized intersections. The east approaches consist of two through lanes, and the north and south 
approaches consist of a through lane. Marked crossings, pedestrian signals, directional curb ramps, and 
DWS are present at each leg of the intersection.  
Lead Avenue & Morningside Drive is a four-legged, three-way, signalized intersection. The east approach 
consists of two through lanes, while the north and south approaches consist of a through lane. Marked 
crossings, pedestrian signals, and DWS are present at each leg of the intersection. Directional curb ramps 
are present at all crosswalks apart from the northwest corner, which is non-directional.  
Lead Avenue and Locust Street is a four-legged, two-way, signalized intersection. The east approach 
consists of a left-turn lane and two through lanes, while the north approach consists of a through lane, a 
shared through/right-turn lane, and a right-turn lane. Marked crossings, pedestrian signals, directional curb 
ramps, and DWS are present at the intersection's west, north, and south legs.  
Lead Avenue & Oak Street is a four-legged, two-way, signalized intersection. The east approach consists of 
three through lanes and a right-turn lane, while the south approach consists of a left-turn lane and two 
through lanes. Marked crossings, pedestrian signals, directional curb ramps, and DWS are present at the 
intersection's east, north, and south legs.

Lead Avenue and University Boulevard is a four-legged, three-way, signalized intersection. The east 
approach consists of two through lanes and a right-turn lane. The north approach consists of three through 
lanes, while the south approach consists of a left-turn lane and three through lanes. Marked crossings, 
pedestrian signals, and directional curb ramps are present at each leg of the intersection.  
Lead Avenue & Yale Boulevard is a four-legged, three-way, signalized intersection. The east approach 
consists of a left-turn lane and two through lanes. The north approach consists of a through lane and a 
yield-controlled channelized right-turn lane, while the south approach consists of a left-turn lane and a 
through lane. Marked crossings, pedestrian signals, and DWS are present at each leg of the intersection. A 
pedestrian refuge island is present on the intersection's northwest corner between the through lanes and 
channelized right turn lane from southbound Yale Boulevard and contains a pedestrian signal. Directional 
curb ramps are present at all crosswalks apart from the southeast corner, which is non-directional.  
Lead Avenue and Girard Boulevard are a four-legged, three-way, signalized intersection. The east approach 
consists of two through lanes, while the north and south approaches consist of a shared through/bicycle 
lane. Marked crossings, pedestrian signals, directional curb ramps, and DWS are present at each leg of the 
intersection. A bicycle lane is present along the north side of Lead Avenue. 
Lead Avenue and Carlisle Boulevard are a four-legged, three-way, signalized intersection. The east 
approach consists of two through lanes. The north approach consists of a through lane, while the south 
approach consists of a left-turn lane and a through lane. Marked crossings, pedestrian signals, directional 
curb ramps, and DWS are present at each leg of the intersection.  
Coal Avenue & Broadway Boulevard is a four-legged, three-way, signalized intersection. The west 
approach consists of a left-turn lane, two through lanes, and a right-turn lane. The north approach consists 
of a left-turn lane and two through lanes, while the south approach consists of two through lanes and a 
shared right-turn/bicycle lane. Marked crossings, pedestrian signals, and DWS are present at each leg of the 
intersection. Directional curb ramps are present on the north corners, while non-directional curb ramps are 
present on the south corners. The marked crossing on the south leg of the intersection is disrupted by a 
median that does not appear to be used as a pedestrian refuge island.   
Coal Avenue & Walter Street is a four-legged, three-way, signalized intersection. The west approach 
consists of two through lanes, while the north and south approaches consist of a through lane. Marked 
crossings, pedestrian signals, and DWS are present at each leg of the intersection. Directional curb ramps 
are present on the north corners, and non-directional curb ramps are present on the south corners.  
Coal Avenue & Spruce Street is a four-legged, three-way, signalized intersection. The west approach 
consists of two through lanes, while the north and south approaches consist of a through lane. Marked 
crossings, pedestrian signals, and DWS are present at each leg of the intersection. Directional curb ramps 
are present at all corners apart from the southeast corner.  
Coal Avenue & Stanford Drive is a four-legged, three-way, signalized intersection. The west approach

The project team approached the study corridor in three segments based on land use, roadway geometry, 
and volume. The segments are shown in Figure 2,

LAND USE 
The study area comprises a few prominent land uses. Segment 1 abuts Low-Density Residential, 
Commercial Retail and Services, Multi-family, and Office primarily. Segment 2 also abuts mostly Low-
Density Residential, Office, Commercial Services, Multi-family, and Educational. Segment 3 is primarily 
adjacent to Low-density Residential areas with some Commercial Retail, Multi-family, Commercial Services, 
and Offices. Figure 3 shows the adjacent land of the study area.  
 
Figure 3: Study Area Adjacent Land Uses

Lead and Coal Studies
 
PEDESTRIAN FACILITIES 
Pedestrian facilities are currently present along the Lead and Coal corridors. The facilities include detached 
sidewalks, ADA ramps, crosswalks, and pedestrian push buttons at each signalized intersection. Segments 
also contain similar pedestrian facility characteristics, including sidewalk widths and attached or detached 
sidewalks. 
Segment 1 
Sidewalks on either side of Lead Avenue within Segment 1 are primarily 7-8 feet. The bicycle lane on the 
north side of Lead Avenue helps to provide a 10-foot buffer, while intermittent parking lanes on the south 
side of Lead Avenue provide a 9-foot buffer for pedestrians. All crosswalks contain marked crossings and 
pedestrian push-buttons at signalized intersections. No benches or pedestrian resting facilities are present. 
Segment 2 
Sidewalks on either side of Lead Avenue within Segment 2 are primarily 7-8 feet and detached. Buffer zones 
on the north side of Lead Avenue are primarily 14 feet, while buffer zones on the south side of Lead Avenue 
vary from 4 feet at the Yale Boulevard intersection to 8-18 feet due to intermittent parking lanes. All 
crosswalks contain marked crossings and pedestrian push-buttons at signalized intersections. There are no 
benches or pedestrian resting facilities within this segment apart from public transit stop locations at Mesa 
Street and Cedar Street. 
Segment 3 
Sidewalks on either side of Lead Avenue within Segment 3 are primarily 7 feet detached. Buffer zones on 
the north side of Lead Avenue range from 6-16 feet, though 12 feet is standard. Buffer zones on the south 
side of Lead Avenue vary from 2-8 feet, though 6-8 feet is standard. All crosswalks contain marked crossings 
and pedestrian push-buttons at signalized intersections. Within this 1.25-mile primarily residential segment, 
there are four benches for pedestrians and three transit stop locations at Yale Boulevard, Girard Boulevard, 
and Carlisle Boulevard, each containing a bench.  
Coal Avenue Pedestrian Facilities 
Segment 1 
Sidewalks on either side of Coal Avenue within Segment 1 are typically 7-8 feet and attached. On the north 
side of Coal Avenue, frequent parking lanes ensure a 10-foot minimum buffer for pedestrians. This is also 
true on the south side of Coal Avenue, where a bicycle lane provides pedestrians with a 10-foot minimum 
buffer. All crosswalks contain marked crossings and pedestrian push-buttons at signalized intersections. No 
pedestrian resting facilities are present. 
Segment 2 
The 6-to-7-foot-wide sidewalks on either side of Coal Avenue within Segment 2 are nearly equally attached 
and detached. On the north side of Coal Avenue, pedestrian buffer zones vary from 4-25 feet due to 
intermittent parking lanes. On the south side of Coal Avenue, pedestrian buffer zones vary from 6-22 feet. 
The bicycle lane present ensures a minimum 6-foot buffer for pedestrians. All crosswalks contain marked 
crossings and pedestrian push-buttons at signalized intersections. Apart from public transit stop locations 
at Spruce Street and University Boulevard, no pedestrian resting facilities are present. 
Segment 3 
Sidewalks on either side of Coal Avenue within Segment 3 are typically 7-8 feet wide and detached. On the 
north side of Coul Avenue, pedestrian buffer zones vary from 0-8 feet, though 4-6 feet is most common. A

BICYCLE FACILITIES 
Bicycle lanes throughout the study area are six feet wide on Lead Avenue and Coal Avenue. Exclusive turn 
lanes are present at Broadway Boulevard, Locust Street, Oak Street, University Boulevard, Yale Boulevard, 
and Washington Street; the bicycle lanes taper to four or five feet wide at these intersections. A four-foot 
buffer is present along the bicycle lanes from Broadway Boulevard to Locust Street.  
TRANSIT 
ABQ Ride Bus Route 97 operates along Lead and Coal Ave. On Lead Avenue, bus stops are available at 
Broadway Boulevard, Elm Street, Cedar Street, Mesa Street, Yale Boulevard, Girard Boulevard, and Carlisle 
Boulevard. On Coal Avenue, bus stops are available at High Street, Mulberry Street, University Boulevard, 
Girard Boulevard, and Carlisle Boulevard.

Turning Movement Counts 
Turning movement counts for the study intersections were collected for three periods: 6:00 AM to 9:00 
AM, 11:00 AM to 2:00 PM, and 3:30 PM to 6:30 PM, in May and June 2024. Turning movement volumes 
collected at the study intersections show a typical commuter-type distribution with observable AM, MD, 
and PM peak hours. The peak hours for the entire study area (network peak) are 7:30 AM – 8:30 AM, 12:00 
PM to 1:00 PM, and 4:30 PM to 5:30 PM. Figure 5 shows the observed peak hours for each intersection 
where traffic counts were collected and the peak hours for the entire study area (network peak). Complete 
turning movement counts can be found in Appendix C. A summary of peak hours by intersection can be 
found in Appendix B. 
 
Figure 5: Turning Movement Counts

SAFETY ASSESSMENT 
Crash Data Limitations 
Crash data is extracted from reports filed with or by law enforcement agencies and is subject to variations 
in reporting based on the officer’s interpretation of the Uniform Crash Report (UCR). Known challenges 
with crash data include excluding crashes below property damage thresholds, unreported crashes, near-
misses, and geolocation accuracy.  
Crash Analysis 
This study analyzed five years of crashes occurring in the study corridor between 2018 and 2022 provided 
by the City of Albuquerque. This crash dataset is the most recent available and contains 1,475 crashes: 751 
on Lead and 724 on Coal. Figure 6 shows a heat map of the reported crashes in the study corridors.
 
Figure 6: Lead & Coal Crash Heat Map (N=1,475), 2018-2022

17

Severity 
The KABCO scale classifies the severity of crashes in New Mexico. The letters in KABCO represent the 
severity of a crash: 
• 
K – Killed (Fatal) 
• 
A – Incapacitated (Serious Injury) 
• 
B – Minor Injury 
• 
C – Complaint of Injury (Suspected Injury)

Crash Summary 
Between 2018 and 2022, crash trends fluctuated, peaking in 2018 before dipping in 2019, followed by a 
30% decline in 2020, likely due to COVID-19-related travel behavior changes. August has the highest crash 
frequency, with peaks in March and June, while fatal crashes peak in November. Crashes increase 
throughout the week, peaking on Fridays, though severe and fatal crashes are most common on Saturdays. 
The highest crash rates occurred at Coal Ave & Carlisle Blvd, Lead Ave & Girard Blvd, and both Oak St 
intersections. Crash frequency mirrors daily traffic patterns, with peaks between 11:00 AM - 12:00 PM and 
3:00 PM - 5:00 PM. Most crashes occurred in daylight or well-lit conditions. Speed was a factor in 
approximately 9% of crashes and resulted in one fatal and four serious injury incidents. Rear-end and T-
bone collisions were the most common impact types from the Manner of Impact data, but this data does 
not represent most of the dataset. Alcohol contributes to 3.5% of crashes in the study corridors and to 
nearly 17% of Fatal and Serious Injury crashes. Additionally, vulnerable road users like pedestrians and 
bicyclists experience disproportionate crash severity.

Predictive Crash Method 
Using the Highway Safety Software (HSS), crash prediction evaluations were performed for the study 
corridors. Table 15 and Table 16 compare the observed, expected, and predicted crash rates for Lead and 
Coal Avenues. Observed crashes are the historical crashes documented in this study's crash data between 
2018 and 2022. The Predictive Method from the Highway Safety Manual (HSM) uses the geometric and 
safety features of each intersection or facility to calculate a Safety Performance Function (SPF) Crash 
Modification Factors (CMF) to estimate a predicted crash frequency. Additionally, HSS uses an Empirical 
Bayes analysis that combines the observed crash frequencies with the predicted crash frequencies from 
similar sites to estimate the expected crash frequency.  The predicted and expected crash frequencies can 
then be compared to the observed annual crashes to identify areas experiencing safety issues. Complete 
reports for both sections from the HSS software can be found in Appendix F. 
New Mexico has lower thresholds for reporting property damage-only crashes at $500 compared to other 
states, such as $1000 in Texas, which may contribute to high crash reporting and, thus, a high expected 
crash rate. New Mexico may have higher reporting rates for property damage-only crashes, higher crash 
frequencies, or a combination of both. Additionally, the segment analyses aggregate crashes from stop-
controlled minor streets and signal-controlled intersections where traffic volume data is unavailable. 
The key takeaway from Table 15 and Table 16 is the observed crash rate exceeds the Predicted and 
Expected crash rates for Lead and Coal Avenues at every intersection and segment analyzed.

SINGLE-LANE OPERATION 
A single-lane operation along the Lead and Coal corridors will reduce the number of east and westbound 
lanes from two to one. One concept for a typical section under a single-lane configuration could comprise a 
buffered 5-foot bicycle lane with a 3-foot buffer, a 10-foot driving lane, and an additional 10-foot buffer, as 
shown in Figure 21The City of Albuquerque’s Development Process Manual indicates that the minimum 
width of a travel lane for all road functional classifications is 10 feet; this lane width is recommended for 
this and subsequent alternatives as a traffic-calming feature.  
Speed cushions should be implemented in the 10-foot buffer to discourage its use during busier times of 
the day. This feature intends to prevent using the buffer space as a passing lane when the road is congested 
while still allowing unobstructed use by emergency vehicles. Likewise, bicyclist safety can be enhanced by 
installing vertical elements inside the buffer, creating a Separated Bicycle Lane. The vertical elements create 
greater separation from motor vehicles and discourage using the wide bicycle lane and buffer as a 
driving/passing lane. However, the recently adopted City of Albuquerque 2024 Bikeway and Trail Facilities 
Plan guidance indicates that vertical separation may not be appropriate for Lead and Coal with frequent 
access points such as intersections, alleyways, and driveways.

As conditions change along the Lead and Coal corridors, some drivers may avoid certain areas and divert to

Initially, the Lomas Boulevard, Central Avenue, Garfield Boulevard, and Gibson Boulevard corridors were 
considered for diversion. However, based on the origin and destination analysis, it was determined that

TRAFFIC ANALYSIS 
The Synchro 12 analysis software was used to analyze the study intersections for Level of Service (LOS) and 
95th percentile queueing conditions. Synchro 12 implements methods and procedures detailed by the 
Highway Capacity Manual (HCM). Detailed capacity output sheets showing all individual movements can be 
found in Appendix E. 
MOTOR VEHICLE LOS, CAPACITY, AND QUEUING ANALYSIS 
Per the HCM, LOS is presented as a letter grade (A through F) based on the calculated average delay for an 
intersection or movement. Delay is calculated as a function of several variables, including signal phasing 
operations, cycle length, traffic volumes, and opposing traffic volumes. Still, it measures the average wait 
time a driver can expect when moving through an intersection. Factors such as total cycle time (for all 
movements), queueing restrictions, and vehicle volumes can affect delay measurements, especially for 
lower-volume movements and side streets. Generally, these factors are only realized when delays reach or 
exceed LOS E thresholds. In such cases, subsequent sections offer a narrative specific to the individual 
movement in question. Traffic counts are in Appendix C. Complete HCM Results Summary Reports are in 
Appendix E. 
Signal timing provided by the City of Albuquerque was used for analysis. The Rest-in-Red operations occur 
during off-peak hours. This study analyzed peak hour periods; therefore, the Rest-in-Red operations did not 
affect the analysis.

Queueing is reported in feet for all intersections with queue lengths greater than one vehicle, with a base 
assumption of 25 feet queue length per vehicle. Queues are reported for queue measurements falling 
within the 95th percentile. Notably, 95th percentile queues are statistically expected to occur during only 5% 
of the peak hour's sign cycles. It is also noted that unreported average queueing at an intersection would 
statistically be much shorter than 95th-percentile queueing. 
The volume-to-capacity (V/C) ratio is a performance measure showing the traffic volume ratio to the lane 
group capacity. A V/C ratio greater than 1.00 indicates that demand creates a residual queue for the 
analysis period. 
For this analysis, acceptable levels of service (LOS) are defined as a LOS D or better. Based on procedures 
outlined in the HCM, intersection delay and level of service for stop-controlled intersections are reported as 
the delay and level of service for the worst-case movement at each intersection. For all other control types, 
they are taken for the whole intersection. Detailed output sheets can be found in Appendix E.

PEDESTRIAN LEVEL OF TRAFFIC STRESS (PLTS) 
PLTS is a qualitative tool to evaluate how comfortable, safe, and accessible a pedestrian facility feels based 
on motor vehicle traffic volume (AADT), traffic speed (85th Percentile), sidewalk width, buffer width, the 
space between motor vehicles and pedestrian facility, i.e., paved shoulder width, bicycle lane, and 
landscaping buffer. It aids in evaluating pedestrian facilities based on stress-inducing factors rather than 
operational attributes, such as a quantitative measure of pedestrian LOS. PLTS uses a tiered system (1-4) to 
rate facilities. The tiers are described as: 
• 
PLTS 1: Little to no stress. Users may include children and elderly individuals. 
• 
PLTS 2: Low stress for most adults but may prove too stressful for some 
• 
PLTS 3: Moderate to high stress discourages walking for many people 
• 
PLTS 4: High stress, not suitable for most users  
PLTS is used because it focuses on factors that make walking uncomfortable or unsafe, while PLOS 
evaluates how efficiently pedestrian facilities function. Figure 52 is the table for road segments with

NOISE ASSESSMENT 
This noise assessment section is organized as follows. The first section discusses vehicle noise 
ordinances and other vehicle noise guidelines from Albuquerque and other jurisdictions to set a frame 
of reference for allowable vehicle noise levels. The data collection process discusses the findings in the 
following and third sections. The final section details different noise mitigation techniques and the pros 
and cons of each. 
VEHICLE NOISE ORDINANCES AND GUIDANCE 
First, Albuquerque's existing vehicle noise ordinance options are discussed. Then, examples of noise 
ordinances and vehicle noise guidance from other jurisdictions are discussed. 
Vehicle Noise Ordinances for Albuquerque 
Several ordinances are aimed at curtailing motor vehicle noise and apply to the City of Albuquerque. We 
first discuss those from the Albuquerque Code of Ordinances, including Albuquerque’s Vehicle Nuisance 
Ordinance (Section 2.1.1.) and Albuquerque’s Traffic Code (Section 2.1.2.). We then discuss the vehicle 
noise ordinance from the Bernalillo County Code (Section 2.1.3.). We finally discuss Albuquerque’s 
general noise ordinance, which is likely inadequate for vehicle noise enforcement (Section 2.1.4.). 
Albuquerque’s Vehicle Nuisance Ordinance (Albuquerque Code of Ordinances; Chapter 7; Article 10) 
The City of Albuquerque’s Vehicle Nuisance Ordinance aims to improve the community's health and 
safety by prohibiting specific motor vehicle driving behaviors, including racing, drag racing, exhibition 
driving, road rage taunting, and other behaviors related to excessive roadway noise. The parts of the 
ordinance most applicable to road noise are provided below:  
§ 7-10-2 FINDINGS AND INTENT. 
(B) The Council further finds that nuisance drivers' vehicles cause considerable property 
damage, bodily harm, and loss of life in the City of Albuquerque. The danger, noise, fear, and 
distraction produced and caused by nuisance drivers lead to immeasurable harm to the 
community. The noise and distraction generated by nuisance vehicles interfere with drivers' 
ability to detect and respond to dangerous or emergency driving conditions and circumstances, 
including but not limited to horn noise and the siren noise of official emergency vehicles. This 
Article aims to abate the nuisance caused by irresponsible drivers' use of cars by employing 
progressive sanctions, including temporary loss or permanent forfeiture of the vehicle. 
§ 7-10-3 VEHICLE NUISANCE - SPECIFIC VIOLATIONS. 
(D) Excessively Loud Electronic Sound or Music. It shall be unlawful for any person or persons to 
play or produce excessively loud sound or music in any vehicle operated on any public street in 
the city limits. For purposes of this section, excessively loud electronic sound or music shall be, 
and the terms shall mean the use of any machine or device for reproducing sound, including any 
magnifying sound instrument used in the production or replication of music, spoken words, or 
other sounds and designed to enlarge the volume of any instrument, voice or other sounds 
including but not limited to radios, stereos or so-called "boom boxes." It shall be a violation of 
this section if any such sound is plainly audible twenty-five feet from the subject vehicle.

(E) Modification of Exhaust Systems. It shall be a violation of this section for any person to 
operate any vehicle within city limits with a modified exhaust system. A modified exhaust 
system shall mean any change or alteration to the exhaust system found on the vehicle when it 
was originally manufactured, and such change results in noise that exceeds the noise the vehicle 
made when manufactured. Any violation of ROA 1994 § 8-6-13 shall also be a violation of this 
paragraph. 
Mitigating excessive road noise from motor vehicles is a goal of the above ordinance. Based on results 
from the noise camera installation as part of this project and from other past noise camera monitoring 
around New Mexico, motor vehicle stereos rarely reach decibel levels that trigger the camera 
(approximately 80 dB(A) or greater), and almost all captures are a result of modified exhaust systems. 
Therefore, the city should likely focus on the exhaust system aspect of the Vehicle Nuisance Ordinance 
instead of the stereo aspect if they wish to maximize excessive motor vehicle noise enforcement. If the 
stereo aspect were enforced, what is “plainly audible” in decibels would likely need to be determined, as 
this is a subjective term. Furthermore, non-modified operating motor vehicles are plainly audible at 
twenty-five feet from the subject vehicle, primarily because of the contact between the vehicle’s tires 
and the roadway; it may, therefore, be of interest to justify why a vehicle is allowed to be plainly audible 
at twenty-five feet, but the stereo is prohibited from being plainly audible at twenty-five feet. 
The exhaust system portion of Albuquerque’s Vehicle Nuisance Ordinance slightly differs from other 
vehicle noise ordinances that largely specify a maximum allowable decibel level. Instead, Albuquerque’s 
ordinance specifies that vehicle exhaust systems are prohibited from making more noise than when they 
were originally manufactured. Enforcement of this ordinance should be possible if stock noise levels can 
be obtained from vehicle manufacturers. However, with a wide range of options available for motor 
vehicles, it may be challenging to identify the noise level of a vehicle’s exhaust system when it was 
originally manufactured. For this reason, vehicle ordinances that specify maximum allowable decibel 
levels (such as Bernalillo County’s Vehicle Noise Ordinance detailed in Section 2.1.3.) may be more 
appropriate. 
Albuquerque’s Traffic Code (Albuquerque Code of Ordinances; Chapter 8; Article 6) 
The City of Albuquerque’s Traffic Code has a section specifically requiring motor vehicles operated 
within city limits to have a muffler in good working order: 
§ 8-6-13 MUFFLERS REQUIRED. 
(A)   Operating Muffler. It shall be unlawful for any person to operate a motor vehicle if it is not 
equipped with a properly attached operating muffler in good working order of construction 
sufficient to prevent excessive or unusual noise of the motor or to muffle or deaden the sound 
from the motor. 
(B)   Muffler Changes or Modification. No person shall modify or change the exhaust muffler, 
intake muffler, or any other noise abatement device of a motor vehicle such that the noise 
emitted by the motor vehicle is increased above that emitted by the motor vehicle as originally 
manufactured. Such prohibited changes or modifications shall include but are not limited to cut-
outs, by-passes, illegal mufflers defined in division (C) below, or other similar devices. 
(C)   Dealers and the like. No person shall sell, offer for sale, install, or offer to install any illegal 
muffler, exhaust cut-out, by-pass, or other device that increases or tends to increase the

83

exhaust noise of a motor vehicle. For this section, an illegal muffler is defined as any straight-
through muffler that does not contain baffles, including but not limited to glass packs, steel 
packs, and straight pipes. 
Albuquerque’s Traffic Code is similar to its Vehicle Nuisance Ordinance, focusing on muffler and exhaust 
systems. However, there is one key benefit to the Traffic Code’s approach in that it is not required to 
prove that a modification has occurred. Whereas enforcement of the Vehicle Nuisance Ordinance would 
require proving that the vehicle’s exhaust system had been modified, the Traffic Code states: “It shall be 
unlawful for any person to operate a motor vehicle if such vehicle is not equipped with a properly 
attached, operating muffler in good working order of construction sufficient to prevent excessive or 
unusual noise of the motor or to muffle or deaden the sound from the motor.” In this way, enforcement 
should be possible without the additional burden of proving that an exhaust system has been modified 
from some previous state. However, the terms “excessive or unusual noise” are still subjective, and it 
would be ideal to have a specific decibel level associated with the criteria. Furthermore, it may need to 
be proven that the observed noise is generated explicitly because of a lack of a muffler.

Bernalillo County’s Vehicle Noise Ordinance avoids many of the abovementioned issues with 
Albuquerque’s ordinances. For instance, while both Albuquerque ordinances detailed above require the 
excessive noise to be coming from a muffler or exhaust system, Bernalillo County’s noise ordinance 
states that: “No person shall operate…a motor vehicle… under any condition of grade, load, acceleration 
or deceleration in such manner as to exceed the following noise limits...” In this way, enforcement is 
possible as long as it can be proven that the noise is coming from the operating motor vehicle without 
requiring identification of the exact source (i.e., exhaust system, stereo, etc.).

providing specific decibel ranges that can be measured objectively. Specific testing criteria are also 
provided to avoid ambiguity further.

made or continued, or allow to be made or continued, any sound that persistently or

A key issue with the general noise ordinance is that the sound must “persistently or continuously” meet 
the specified decibel levels. An operating motor vehicle may only meet those decibel levels briefly at any 
monitoring location before driving off. Furthermore, the decibel levels are low enough for most 
unmodified standard passenger vehicles to surpass them. Therefore, General noise ordinances are not 
tailored for enforcing excessive motor vehicle noise.

NOISE DATA COLLECTION 
We first detail the collection of decibel levels using sound level meters. We then detail the identification 
of vehicle types with a noise camera. 
Decibel Level Data Collection with Sound Level Meters 
Sound level meters were used to collect sound level measurements in A-weighted decibels (dB(A)) at 
eight locations along the Lead/Coal corridor: Lead & Solano (location #1 in Figure 63), Lead & Tulane 
(#2), Lead & Cornell (#3), Lead & Buena Vista (#4), Lead & Mulberry (#5), Lead & Edith (#6), Coal & 
Cornell (#7), and Coal & Amherst (#8). The sound level meters were installed approximately 15 feet 
above ground level on utility poles located as closely as possible to the locations noted in Figure 63. 
Collections were taken for about 53 hours between approximately 8:00 AM on Tuesday, September 24, 
2024, and 1:00 PM on Thursday, September 26, 2024.

89 
Lead and Coal Studies 
 
 
Figure 63: Lead/Coal Avenue Sound Level Monitoring Locations 
REED R8070SD Data Logging Sound Level Meters were utilized for noise monitoring. These meters are 
certified to Type 2 standards (± 1.0 dB) according to IEC 61672-1-2013. The sound level meters were 
calibrated immediately before deployment in the field and were confirmed to still be within ±0.1 dB(A) 
when uninstalled. Each sound level meter recorded one dB(A) reading every second throughout the 
study period. 
The data was then processed to identify the number of high-noise events (e.g., noise events above 80 
dB(A) and noise events above 90 dB(A)) at each monitoring location, as well as the average decibel 
levels throughout the study period. Distinct noise events were differentiated using a four-second gap. In 
other words, take as a hypothetical situation that a single loud vehicle driven by a sound level meter 
produced decibel readings above 80 dB(A) for six seconds, which would result in six readings above 80 
dB(A). Instead of counting this as six high-noise events, we counted all immediately subsequent 
≥80dB(A) readings as a single event until there was a gap of at least four seconds between ≥80dB(A) 
readings. 
It should be noted that while sound level meters can record decibel levels, they cannot identify the 
noise source. In other words, while the sound level meters identified high-noise events along the study 
roadways, and one could reasonably assume that those high-noise events may be primarily caused by

90

operating motor vehicles, it is possible that some of the high-noise events recorded by the sound level 
meters were caused by other noise sources (e.g., gunshots, leaf blowers, etc.). Because of the inability of 
sound level meters to identify noise sources, a noise camera was also installed in the corridor. 
Vehicle Type Identification with Noise Camera 
A noise camera was also installed during the monitoring period between approximately 11:00 AM on 
Tuesday, September 24, 2024, and 1:30 PM on Thursday, September 26, 2024. The noise camera was 
installed on Coal Avenue between Cornell Drive SE and Stanford Drive SE, approximately 24 feet from 
the centerline of the traveled way and within 300 feet of monitoring location #7 from Figure 63. 
The noise camera consisted of a camera that was triggered whenever an 80 dB(A) threshold was 
surpassed. The camera’s video capture and noise source localization allowed for identifying the noise 
source for each high-noise event during the study period. If the noise source was a motor vehicle, the 
vehicle type (e.g., heavy vehicles, pickup trucks, motorcycles, sports cars, etc.) of the noise source could 
be identified in the video capture. The license plate camera was not enabled during this study to avoid 
privacy issues. Identifying the vehicle type will inform whether further enforcement of truck restrictions 
may help improve noise pollution along the corridors.

NOISE MITIGATION TECHNIQUES 
The guidance below regarding noise mitigation techniques was largely based on FHWA’s Highway Traffic 
Noise: Analysis and Abatement Guidance.  Traffic noise abatement techniques approved by FHWA 
include noise barriers, managing traffic (including truck restrictions), vegetation, and installing noise 
insulation in buildings. Note that while the guidance is for highways, applying techniques to urban areas 
is discussed and, therefore, may apply to the study. 
Noise Barriers 
Noise barriers are the most prevalent form of noise abatement. Noise barriers are solid obstructions 
built between the roadway and the noise receivers. Effective noise barriers can reduce noise levels by 10 
decibels. While noise barriers may effectively mitigate noise, they are inappropriate in all contexts. 
FHWA details context considerations that are likely applicable to the Lead/Coal corridor: 
“A major consideration in the design of a noise barrier is the visual impact on the adjoining land 
use. An important concern is the scale relationship between the barrier and activities along the 
roadway right-of-way. A tall barrier near a low-scale single-family detached residential area 
could have a severe adverse visual effect. In addition, a tall barrier placed close to residences 
could create detrimental shadows. One solution to the potential problem of scale relationship is 
to provide staggered horizontal elements to a noise barrier to reduce the visual impact through 
the introduction of landscaping in the foreground. This can also allow for additional sunlight and 
air movement in the residential area. In general, it is desirable to locate a noise barrier 
approximately four times its height from residences and to provide landscaping near the barrier 
to avoid visual dominance.” 
Given the limited right-of-way along the Lead/Coal corridor and the residential context, noise barriers 
are likely not a realistic solution for noise abatement.

94 
Lead and Coal Studies 
 
Traffic Control (Including Truck Restrictions) 
FHWA also recommends traffic control methods for noise mitigation, including: 
1. Prohibiting trucks from certain streets and roads, 
2. Permitting trucks to use certain streets and roads only during daylight hours, 
3. Timing traffic lights to achieve smooth traffic flow and eliminate the need for frequent 
acceleration and deceleration, 
4. Reducing speed limits reduces traffic noise levels; however, an approximate reduction of 20 
mph is necessary for a readily perceptible decrease in noise levels. 
Given the findings above from the noise cameras regarding the relatively few motor vehicles violating 
the existing truck restrictions, further truck restrictions or further enforcement of existing truck 
restrictions will likely not significantly ameliorate the noise issues observed on the Lead/Coal corridor. 
The noise issues observed at the study site were not related to signal timing, and further reducing the 
speed limit by the recommended 20 MPH was not feasible in the study corridor. Therefore, the traffic 
control noise mitigation techniques suggested by FHWA are likely not applicable solutions for the 
observed Lead/Coal noise issues. 
Vegetation 
FHWA suggests vegetation as a possible noise mitigation technique, although they note that vegetation 
is infrequently feasible given the width and density of vegetation required to dampen noise. For 
instance, FHWA estimates that a 200-foot width of dense vegetation would be required to reduce noise 
by 10 decibels (Figure 66). Planting trees and shrubs may provide psychological benefits by providing 
visual screening, but it typically does not function as noise abatement. Vegetation is, therefore, not a 
feasible noise mitigation technique for the Lead/Coal corridor. 
 
Source: FHWA Highway Traffic Noise: Analysis and Abatement Guidance 
 
Figure 66: Vegetation as Noise Mitigation Technique  
Noise Insulation 
The final noise mitigation technique suggested by FHWA is noise insulation installed directly on or in 
affected buildings. However, FHWA notes that highway agencies typically only consider noise insulation 
for public use or nonprofit institutional structures (e.g., places of worship, schools, hospitals, libraries,

95 
Lead and Coal Studies 
 
etc.). Directly modifying private residences is not a standard procedure and is likely not a noise 
mitigation approach that is pertinent for a city. Therefore, it is likely that none of the above standard 
noise mitigation techniques detailed by FHWA are appropriate to the Lead/Coal corridor. 
Automated Noise Enforcement 
Although not mentioned by the FHWA, automated noise enforcement via noise cameras may be an 
effective approach for the Lead/Coal corridor. Noise cameras, such as the unit used for vehicle type 
identification in this study, constantly measure decibel levels along a roadway and are triggered when a 
set decibel threshold is surpassed. The noise camera can localize the noise source to confirm which 
motor vehicle is generating the offending noise and identify the individual vehicle via a license plate 
camera. In addition, decibel levels and audio are recorded throughout each capture to provide 
additional evidence. 
Noise cameras are a relatively new technology and are not yet widely used in the United States. New 
York City is the only known municipality issuing citations based on noise camera data, although several 
other cities have completed noise camera pilot programs. To successfully mitigate vehicle noise along 
the Lead/Coal corridor with noise cameras, the city would need to issue warnings or citations to vehicle 
owners violating any of the applicable ordinances detailed above.

SPEED MITIGATIONS 
Reduced Speed Limit (25 MPH) in Primary Residential Areas 
Lowering the speed limit to 25 MPH may reduce the kinetic energy involved in a crash on Lead and Coal 
Avenues; this is subject to speed limit compliance by motorists. By slowing vehicles down, motorists 
have more time to react to unexpected situations, increasing their ability to avoid crashes. Lower speeds 
also reduce the required stopping distance, minimizing the risk of collisions. The combined effect of 
reduced impact force and increased reaction time makes the lower speed limit critical in creating safer 
roads for everyone. Reducing the speed limit is low-cost and can be implemented quickly. Still, it should 
be considered with other countermeasures since arbitrarily lowering the posted speed limit will not 
yield the desired impact on driver behavior.  
Dynamic Speed Feedback Signs 
Dynamic Speed Feedback Signs include radar that captures and displays the approaching vehicle’s 
speed. They may be solar-powered, which can reduce the cost of powering the sign. However, it is 
recommended that consistency in the placement of the Speed Feedback signs be maintained to prevent 
speeds from rebounding once the signage ends. Figure 68 depicts the configuration of a Speed Feedback 
Sign.

Narrow Driving Lanes to 10 feet 
Lane width and motor vehicle speed are related. Narrower lanes aim to slow vehicle speeds and 
increase speed limit compliance. As shown in Figure 69, narrower lanes tend to reduce vehicle speeds at 
a rate of 3 MPH for every foot reduction in driving lane width1.

Intersection Gateway Treatments 
Delineator posts are vertical elements that guide motorists or restrict the travel path. They may include 
a strip of reflectorized plastic to increase visibility in low-light conditions. For the Lead and Coal 
corridors, vertical elements may encourage motorists to slow down by adding to the road's visual 
friction and highlighting the lane's narrowness. Additionally, they create a perceived barrier to crossing 
the centerline. This measure aims to create a safer environment by encouraging more cautious driver 
behavior. Vertical centerline elements contribute to a safer road environment by calming traffic and 
discouraging unsafe vehicle maneuvers. Motor vehicles often damage vertical elements and may lead to 
undesirable maintenance costs.  
6-inch Lane Striping 
Wide lane striping can aid driver awareness and emphasize roadway delineation by enhancing the 
visibility of travel lane boundaries. Lane striping with a six or eight-inch width is considered wide. They 
can provide a safety benefit to all facility types. Additionally, wide lane striping may provide better 
guidance for autonomous vehicles. Furthermore, wide lane striping may increase the narrow

appearance of a travel lane. To distinctly demarcate the bicycle facility, wide striping is recommended 
between bicycle lanes (and bicycle lane buffers) and motor vehicle lanes, and to highlight intersections, 
wide lane striping is recommended at unsignalized intersection approaches. 
LEFT-TURNS FROM RIGHT-LANE (VICE VERSA) 
Install Thru-Left and Thru-Right Combo Arrow Pavement Markings  
Thru-left and Thru-right combo arrow pavement markings on a one-way street enhance safety by 
guiding motorists on their permitted movements, minimizing confusion and potential conflicts at 
intersections. These markings help prevent last-minute lane changes by communicating the allowed 
vehicle movements. Additionally, they may reduce the risk of sideswipe and rear-end collisions by 
ensuring predictable driver behavior.  
Solid White / Double Solid White Center Stripes on Intersection Approaches  
Solid /Double solid white center stripes at an intersection approach may enhance safety by delineating 
the traffic lanes. These markings help maintain predictable and organized traffic flow by reinforcing lane 
geometry. They also improve driver awareness by visually reinforcing an intersection and the need to be 
in the appropriate for the motorists' desired movement designated lane as they approach the 
intersection. By preventing erratic lane shifts, this striping may contribute to a more predictable driving 
environment, enhancing safety for all road users. 
RED LIGHT RUNNING 
Reflective Signal Head Backplates 
Reflective signal backplates enhance the visibility of traffic signals, making them much easier to see, 
especially under low-light conditions. Think of them like high-visibility vests for traffic signals. By 
catching and reflecting headlight beams, they grab a driver's attention sooner and highlight an 
upcoming intersection. This extra visibility reduces confusion and the likelihood of red light running. 
Ultimately, this countermeasure can make intersections safer for motorists, pedestrians, and bicyclists 
by improving traffic signals' clarity and conspicuity. This countermeasure is one of FHWA's Proven Safety 
Countermeasures that may reduce all crash types by up to 15%2.  
Advanced Vehicle Detection and ‘Red Protect’ Operations 
Advanced Vehicle Detection and ‘Red Protect’ operations can enhance signalized intersection safety by 
using technology to detect approaching vehicles and adjust traffic signals accordingly, reducing the 
likelihood of red-light running and crashes. Advanced vehicle detection can extend the green duration 
for vehicles that may be forced into sudden stops, preventing rear-end crashes. It also prioritizes cross-
traffic and pedestrian safety by ensuring signals respond dynamically to current traffic conditions. The 
‘Red Protect’ feature enhances safety by holding the red light for conflicting movements when a 
potential hazard is detected, reducing the risk of side-impact or T-bone collisions. These technologies 
may create a safer environment by minimizing unexpected conflicts.

Bicycle Lane Buffer 
The corridors' existing conditions include bicycle lanes. Enhancing the existing facilities with a buffer and 
reducing the travel lane width would provide additional separation from motor vehicles.

Vertical elements can be used to highlight conflict points at intersections. 
Green Bicycle Boxes 
Green bicycle box pavement markings highlight conflict points at intersections. 
Daylighting on side streets to define intersections 
Daylighting refers to removing visual obstructions such as parked cars, signs, or overgrown vegetation 
near intersections, crosswalks, and driveways to improve visibility between road users. Daylighting 
treatments on local streets that intersect with collectors or arterials can act as a gateway treatment and 
communicate a transition between road environments, encouraging slower turning speeds and tighter 
curb radii. Daylighting may be accomplished using paint and post or curb extensions. Daylighting may aid 
with speed limit compliance and create a safer road environment on minor street north and south 
approaches at Lead and Coal Avenues.

SUMMARY STATEMENTS  
This study was completed to supplement the 2022 Road Safety Audit (RSA) conducted by the Federal 
Highway Administration (FHWA). The RSA identified 19 recommendations to enhance safety; four 
initiatives were advanced and formed the foundational scope used herein. 
This report is provided to the Lead and Coal Working Group, which was established in November of 
2022. The data and analysis provided herein aim to aid in decision-making by residents, the Mayor’s 
administration, the City of Albuquerque’s Department of Municipal Development, the District 6 City 
Councilor, and the Albuquerque Police Department.  
This study builds on the RSA by providing a detailed analysis of the four initiatives:  
• 
Reducing the Posted Speed Limit to 25 MPH, 
• 
Single-lane Operation, 
• 
Two-way Operation and a 
• 
Noise Assessment.  
This report documents the study's findings to guide the Lead and Coal Working Group in making 
informed, data-driven decisions about the future of these corridors.  As such, this report is not intended 
to provide recommendations but to provide insight into the pros and cons of the alternatives, provide 
additional crash data insight, and prepare cost estimates for the Lead and Coal Taskforce and the 
encompassing Working Group’s use. A decision matrix tool was developed to assist the Taskforce and 
Working Group in reviewing the alternatives, as shown in Table 28 below.  
Stopping short of recommendations, the project team offers the following insights: 
• 
Speed reduction most applies to the residential areas west of the I-25 and east of Yale. 
o A speed reduction from I-25 to Yale is viable, but the trade-offs in connectivity to the 
hospital and university areas should be recognized. 
o The Speed Reduction Alternative can be blended with other alternatives. 
• 
The Single Lane Alternative from I-25 to Yale degrades to unacceptable levels for vehicle Level of 
Service (delays) and Queuing. 
o The Single Lane Alternative provides the most significant impact and opportunity to 
benefit Bicycle and Pedestrian Levels of Traffic Stress. 
• 
The Two-way Operation alternative is the most expensive and complex to implement. 
Considerable improvements would be required at the I-25 interchanges and the Washington 
Street junction.

The Noise Assessment concluded that commercial and heavy vehicles are not significant

RE Lead and Coal Studies: Road Safety and Standard of Care 
 
As you head towards concluding the Lead and Coal Studies, I recommend that you make clear 
-and make clear in your final report- what the scope of work is regarding any examination of the 
safety of the Lead-Coal roadway (ie “road safety”). I also recommend that you make clear to the 
community what any relevant engineering standard of care may be regarding the need for a 
road safety study in this matter. 
 
As I understand the scope of the Lead and Coal Studies, it does not look at whether the 
Lead-Coal roadway is safe: not in its entirety, not for any section, and not for any site-specific 
location.The study is blind to the question. It appears to assume, without stating such, that the 
roadway itself is safe.  
 
If this is the case, then, I recommend you not represent in the study report that you have looked 
at the safety of the roadway. Your look at “comparable” roadways or your singling out of any 
specific feature of Lead-Coal between Washington St and Yale Blvd and citing that the same 
feature is found in other settings (for example that “homes on Indian School are also 15 feet 
away from the roadway”) does not constitute a road safety study. 
 
If the current study does not itself look at the safety of the Lead-Coal roadway, I encourage you 
to refer to any previous examination of road safety, including -and specifically-  for the section 
from Washington to Yale. In my 20 year experience as a citizen advocate for Lead-Coal no such 
study has ever been done. 
 
Moreover, not only has a road study never been done, the City of Albuquerque (CABQ) and the 
Department of Municipal Development (DMD) have repeatedly evaded a road safety study of  
Lead-Coal: in the $32M federally funded Lead and Coal Avenues Improvements Project (safety 
document 2010); in the $120M federally funded Albuquerque Rapid Transit Project (safety 
document 2015); in Mayor Keller’s December 2019 cancellation of an already requested FHWA 
1

Road Safety Audit (RSA) on Lead-Coal from Washington to Yale; and in the 2022 FHWA RSA 
which, as a “pedestrian” audit, precluded any look at conditions of the roadway. 
 
It is demonstrably unsafe to operate a high volume, high speed roadway -to operate two lanes 
of busy traffic whether unidirectional or bidirectional- on our narrow residential side streets. If it 
is safe –if there’s nothing to hide– why has CABQ repeatedly evaded a full, unbiased look at 
road safety as a factor in the crash problem on our roadway section? 
 
If the current study is not looking at road safety and there is no previous road safety study to 
refer to, you are then necessarily constrained in the scope of your final report. Your analysis 
must focus on and clearly state to what extent any mitigation measure will do what the FHWA to 
its credit made clear in its 2022 report is the purpose of this exercise: make Lead and Coal 
Avenues safe for the people who live, walk and bike alongside them. Or, to express that 
purpose in the vernacular: keep the damn cars on the road. 
 
1. Absent a road safety study, you have no basis to conclude that for the roadway from 
Washington to Yale (the section of intense community concern since January 2018) the current 
traffic configuration –or even its tweaked, “enhanced safety” version– is safe. Again, it is 
demonstrably not.   
 
2. Absent a road safety study, you have no basis to conclude that the bidirectional option would 
be safe, or safer than the current configuration. A priori, the significant sightline obstruction 
present all along the Washington to Yale section would be as bad or worse in a bidirectional 
configuration. 
 
3. You do have a basis to conclude that the single lane option would, by many factors, best 
protect the safety of residents, pedestrians and bicyclists 24/7/365 along the Washington to Yale 
section.  
 
4. Absent a road safety study, you have no basis to refute or dismiss the FHWA’s conclusion 
that a 25 mph speed limit -of course, strictly managed- is indicated to keep the cars on the road. 
And, you have no basis to refute the sustained, and well substantiated community 
recommendation for a 25 mph speed limit in the Washington to Yale section. 
 
So, please, clarify your scope and adhere to it. You may reasonably acknowledge the absence 
of a road safety study. I strongly suggest you do so in your report.  You may not imply that the 
roadway is safe and that the demolition derby outside our homes is just on the drivers.  And, the 
conclusions in your report must be laser focused on what measures will work best to keep 
residents, pedestrians, and cyclists safe. 
 
Finally,  Lee Engineering (in this study) and DMD (in its decades long management of crash 
safety on Lead-Coal) give the appearance of treating a critical crash safety problem without an 
adequate diagnostic examination. What is the relevant engineering standard of care here?  
When is a “road safety” study indicated?  
2

We all look forward to putting the Lead-Coal matter to rest, finally. Beyond a definitive safety 
solution, that will necessitate learning why it has taken CABQ decades to fix the problem. If a 
road safety study should have been done decades ago, the community deserves to know that. 
 
Thank you for your work. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Joseph Aguirre
